rationale: The book's core redefinition of 'sign' as an advance prophecy (oracle/scene/lived prophetic story) whose fulfillment later testifies—and its explicit exclusion of a wonder performed on demand—selectively fits the three printed references and a subset of prophetic-act texts, but requires special pleading for the many passages in which the performed miracle itself is immediately designated the sign that authenticates and produces faith. The broader functional common interpretation (a perceptible act/event/object, characteristically miraculous, that points beyond itself to divine activity, authenticates a messenger, or seals a covenant) accounts for every example the book cites as special cases while also covering the dominant 'signs and wonders' collocations, the Johannine usage, and the Exodus authentication texts with fewer unsupported restrictions. The chapter's own admission that John calls the feeding a sēmeion underscores the tension rather than resolving it.
book_core_identification: A prophecy given in advance—often a prophet's lived story—whose fulfillment testifies; not a wonder performed on demand.
book_secondary_elaborations: Covenant markers (rainbow, circumcision, Sabbath, Passover blood) as a second, non-forward-pointing family of signs
Two Deuteronomic validity tests (fulfillment + consistency with the law/first commandment)
Equation of signs with prophetic similitudes (lived likenesses composed by God)
Extension of the method to all biblical history as typological prophecy (Abraham/Isaac, Joseph, Israel, Rahab, etc.)
Claim that 'there is no wonder in it anywhere' on the day a true sign is given
strongest_counter_interpretation: A sign is a visible act, event, object or miracle that points beyond itself to God's presence, power, purpose or message—most characteristically a miraculous work that authenticates God's messenger and reveals divine identity, calling observers to faith (paradigmatically the Johannine signs and the Exodus signs-and-wonders).
counter_core_identification: A perceptible (often miraculous) pointer/authenticator of divine activity, message or messenger.
material_core_denial: The book denies that a performed wonder constitutes a biblical sign and insists the sign is only the advance prophetic word or lived story whose later fulfillment supplies the testimony; the counter holds that the wonder/act itself is frequently the sign.
counter_case: John 2:11 immediately calls the Cana miracle 'the beginning of signs' that manifested glory and produced belief, with no advance-prophecy frame required
Acts 2:22 and Hebrews 2:3-4 treat 'signs and wonders' as the performed works that attested Jesus and the apostolic word
Exodus 4:1-9 and 7:3 present the signs given to Moses as the on-the-spot wonders (staff-to-snake, etc.) that authenticate
The frequent collocation 'signs and wonders' treats signs as belonging to the category of miraculous attestation

Even the book's preferred examples (Ezekiel as sign, Isaiah's nakedness, Jonah) remain visible enacted acts that point and authenticate, fitting the broader pointer definition without needing to exclude wonders
Deuteronomy 13:1-3 still calls a performed wonder a 'sign' even when it is later judged invalid by the second test
book_explanatory_advantages: Fits Isaiah 7:14 exactly: the sign is the spoken word, no wonder occurs that day, fulfillment arrives centuries later
Fits Ezekiel 24:24 and Luke 11:30 where the prophet's own experience/story is the sign
Explains Jesus' refusal of a demanded sign except the sign of Jonah
Unifies oracle-signs and lived prophetic dramas under the 'when this comes to pass you will know' formula
counter_explanatory_advantages: Covers the entire semantic range (miracles, covenant tokens, eschatological portents, prophetic acts) under one functional umbrella without arbitrary exclusion of wonders
Requires no redefinition of the dominant 'signs and wonders' usage or of Johannine miracle-signs
Matches the consensus of the three independent common-interpretation responses and standard biblical lexicography
Handles false signs (Deut 13, Matt 24:24, 2 Thess 2:9) naturally: the performed wonder is still called a sign
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: John 2:11 (and parallel Johannine texts) in which a wonder performed on the occasion is itself the 'sign' that immediately testifies, without being an earlier prophecy whose later fulfillment is required
The repeated pairing 'signs and wonders' (Deut 4:34, Acts 2:22, Heb 2:4, etc.) that places signs inside the category of performed miraculous works
Mark 16:17-20 and Acts passages where 'signs' are the miracles that accompany believers and confirm the word, not advance prophecies
decisive_sources: John 6:14 (book's own admission that the performed feeding is a sēmeion)
unresolved_objections: The book correctly isolates a real and under-emphasized biblical usage (advance prophetic oracles and lived prophetic dramas) that should not be collapsed into 'miracle' alone
The distinction between demanded wonders and the sign of Jonah has clear Synoptic support
Covenant signs are cleanly integrated by the book as a second family
